title: Improved light conditions sustain pelagic primary production in western Wadden Sea despite biomass declines under major nutrient reductions
content:
Abstract

Pelagic microalgae supply the major part of labile and readily accessible organic carbon in coastal systems, making long-term monitoring of phytoplankton blooms and primary production (PP) essential for assessing the Wadden Sea's carrying capacity. Over the past three decades (1990–2023), our phenology analysis indicates that both the spring and summer-autumn phytoplankton blooms declined in peak magnitude, and secondary blooms shifted later in the season (≈ 40 d over 34 years). These changes coincided with strong reductions in riverine nutrient loads (TN −64%; TP −93%), which were positively correlated with summer phytoplankton biomass. We leveraged one of the longest and methodologically consistent coastal PP time series to identify major patterns and drivers for the western Wadden Sea. Limitation analysis for 2012–2023 showed that phosphorus was the primary limiting nutrient, with silicate co-limitation during spring peaks and nitrogen limitation emerging later in the season. Estimated pelagic PP (mgC m−2 d−1) during the main growth period (May–September) remained relatively stable over 2012–2023, despite a 56% decline in phytoplankton biomass (mg Chl-a m−3). This stability reflects a compensatory increase (170%) in derived phytoplankton growth rates (gC gC−1 d−1), likely facilitated by improved early-season light conditions (≈ 17% increase in March–April). The compensatory balance between declining biomass and increasing growth appears fragile. If nutrient loads further decline and/or light conditions shift beyond the optimum range, the compensatory growth may become insufficient to offset biomass declines. The result would be reduced pelagic primary production and a lower carrying capacity of the ecosystem.
